# Fit a random-effects model

Now we fit the mixed-effects model: a population-level regression **plus** random
intercepts for each group (reef/site).

## The model

Here's an example of a random effects model. Pay attention, in a minute I'll ask you to re-write this for a new dataset. 

$$
y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\ \sigma), \qquad

\mu_i = \alpha + \beta\,x_i + b_{\text{group}[i]}, \qquad

b_j \sim \text{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_b)
$$

In FANGS:

```
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sigma)
    mu[i] <- alpha + beta * x[i] + b[group[i]]
  }
  for (j in 1:J) {
    b[j] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
  }
  alpha   ~ dnorm(0, 50)
  beta    ~ dnorm(0, 10)
  sigma   ~ dunif(0, 50)
  sigma.b ~ dunif(0, 50)
}
```

`alpha + beta * x[i]` is the fixed effect part of the model, that drives the mean in response to a covariate `x`. 

`b[group[i]]` are the group means. Note how each value is drawn from a shared distribution with a SD that is estimated: `b[j] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)`. This is what makes it a random effect. 

Compare to the fixed effect parameter `beta` which is drawn directly from a prior. 

The SD for the `sigma.b` prior (50) is what we call a hyper-parameter, a parameter that controls other parameters. Lower values of the SD will shrink our random effects closer to the global mean. 

Other differences to note in the model definition from earlier models: 

- `J` — the number of groups. Set it in the constants alongside `N`.
- `group[i]` — which group observation `i` belongs to (FANGS encodes a text
  column for you).

## Run the model 

Go to FANGS and click the preset options for 'Load example data' and 'mixed-effects model'. It will load up this data. Run the model and inspect the results. 

Note that it will only show trace plots for the scalar parameters (single values), click the tick-box at the top of the trace plot panel if you want to see traces for the `b` parameter (which is an array). 

## What to check

The **Summary** tab now includes $\sigma_b$ and each `b[j]`. Watch R-hat for
$\sigma_b$ especially — variance parameters are the slowest to mix.

## Your task

Fit the random-intercepts model to `random-effects.csv` and check $\alpha$,
$\beta$, and the group SD $\sigma_b$. 

A few tips: don't forget to change the variable names for the new dataset; you will need to update the distribution for the response variable (its count data...); don't forget to enter a value for J, the number of sites.
